item.title: ‘Thank you, Test Cricket’: Mohammed Shami retires from longest format of the game
item.description: NEW DELHI: Fast bowler Mohammed Shami has retired from Test cricket, closing a 13-year career in the longest format with an emotional message on Instagram on Friday night. The announcement came exactly 13 years after his Test debut. Shami first played for India in the format on 6 November 2013, against West Indies in Kolkata. “I am bidding farewell to the white jersey, but never to the memories associated with it,” Shami wrote. Recalling his first Test cap, he added: “When I wore India’s Test jersey for the first time, I had only one dream — to do something for my country. Since then, every wicket, every struggle, every injury, and every comeback has taught me something.” He described the format as far more than a place to play. “Test cricket has not just been a format for me, it has been a deeply special part of my life,” Shami further noted. “Today, with a heavy heart and countless beautiful memories, I am announcing my retirement from Test cricket.” — MdShami11 (@MdShami11) The 36-year-old thanked the people around him, from “every teammate, coach, family member, and the millions of Indians who supported me on this journey, and who kept their faith in me through both good times and bad.” He also named the BCCI and the Cricket Association of Bengal, his home association, for backing him early. “A sincere thank you as well to the BCCI and the Cricket Association of Bengal (CAB) for believing in my talent, giving me opportunities to grow, and playing a vital role in my cricketing journey. Your support and trust will always remain special to me.” Shami finishes with 229 wickets from 64 Tests, including six five-wicket hauls and best figures of 6/56. His last Test was the June 2023 match against Australia. In the same year he was the leading wicket-taker at the ODI World Cup, with 24 wickets in seven innings. He closed his message on a personal note. “Even though my final Test ball has been bowled on the field, the pride of playing for India will always remain alive in my heart. Thank you, Test Cricket.”

item.title: ‘Stop playing games’: SEC reportedly considering luxury tax for schools that overspend on players
item.description: Kirby Lee-USA TODAY Sports The SEC might be borrowing an idea from professional sports. The conference is reportedly considering a luxury tax on schools that spend more on their players than the revenue-sharing cap allows. A working group of SEC athletic directors, university presidents, and general counsels has been discussing the idea for the past few weeks. The league could vote on it soon, with the hope of having it in place before football’s early signing period in December. The revenue-sharing cap Under the House v. NCAA settlement, schools are allowed to pay their athletes directly through revenue sharing, up to a set cap. That cap is $21.3 million for the 2026-27 academic year and will rise to about $22.2 million in 2027-28. Schools have found ways to spend beyond that, though. Much of the extra money gets routed through third-party NIL deals, which makes it hard for anyone to know what their competitors are actually paying. The SEC isn’t the only conference trying to rein that in. Last month, the Big Ten adopted a conference rule limiting its schools’ involvement in third-party NIL deals, ahead of the possible passage of the Protect College Sports Act in Congress. The PCSA would increase the amount schools can pay players directly by $27.5 million. It’s now unclear whether Congress will pass it after Tuesday’s elections. ‘People stop playing games’ According to ESPN’s Mark Schlabach and Pete Thamel, one formula the SEC is considering would gradually tax schools once they go over the cap. For example, a school could be taxed 1% for spending $1 million over the cap and 3% for spending $3 million over. The details are still being worked out, and some schools want to keep the penalty as low as possible. “Some schools want it to be where the penalty is as low as possible, so it’s cheap enough to where you’re more motivated just to pay it directly and report it, and everybody’s on the same page and people stop playing games,” a source said, via ESPN . The goal is to discourage overspending, while also giving schools a clearer picture of what everyone else is paying. The SEC also hopes it would cut down on the need for third parties to “wash” the money. “It’s a lot better if we all know what everybody’s doing right now,” a source told ESPN. “We’re living in this world where we have no idea what anybody’s spending. Agents can play you all day long because there is no general database. We’re starting to get some information, but there’s not enough transparency to know what people are really doing.” We’ll have to see whether or not the SEC actually moves forward with this plan. item.title: Hamlin and Bell left with what could have been in NASCAR Chase
item.description: Motorsport photo Statistically, Kyle Larson has a 99.4 percent chance of winning the NASCAR Cup Series championship on Sunday at Homestead-Miami Speedway, leaving Christopher Bell and Denny Hamlin at a combined .6 percent. In short, either of them coming back to win the Chase for the Championship would amount to the most improbable comeback in the history of a stock car season finale, so they are not holding their figurative breath. All Larson has to do is finish 28th on Sunday but that assumes he fails to score a single stage point as well. Each stage point he earns over the first half of the race lowers that bare minimum clinch spot by one. He could put the championship away prior to halfway by scoring eight stage points. In other words, a third-place finish in stage one ends the championship. Fourth and eighth over the first two stages ends it. So how much confidence does Hamlin have in his .3 odds? "I mean, I don't have any optimism," Hamlin said. "I don't. I'm here to try to have fun and try to win the race if possible, but I don't … I mean, there's obviously a chance you can win the lottery as well, but do you really count on that?" Bell added that he ‘doesn’t know what else to say,’ because the odds are the odds. Read Also: Kyle Larson sits alone on stage for NASCAR Championship Media Day How Kyle Larson can lose the NASCAR Cup championship at Homestead For Hamlin, this Chase for the Championship was especially frustrating because he entered as the top seeded contender and had four regular season wins. It was a championship he controlled from the summer through the Bristol Night Race. It's all he wanted after being two laps away from winning the championship last year under the final four format before a caution took that one away too. "I felt like last year was like a sudden death and this one was just a slow bleed, truthfully," Hamlin said. "I mean, that's really was how it was. I mean, I was in shock for 10 minutes after the checkered flag waved because I hadn't seen (Larson) all day and now he's suddenly ahead of me. "And then this year, through each playoff race, I'm on the way home just thinking, 'Gosh, it's alright though. We'll have to just make up for it next week.' And then we've just been trickling along and staying somewhat mathematically possible by being solid, but this one was definitely a cut to the wrist and we just watched it bleed." While Larson has taken control of the championship with his three playoff wins and second most stage points earned over the past nine races, Bell and Hamlin also endured mistakes that could have made this a lot closer. “Ultimately, I think whenever we got into The Chase, the 5 car had a pickup in performance, but I still think by the numbers, there have been guys in Toyota cars specifically that have been faster than them, but just we all shot ourselves in a foot one way or the other,” Bell said. The Brewers have a chance to be more than just a one-and-done championship team. Almost all of their key players are under contract for next season and beyond, and they are a very young team that is expected to only get better. However, it's impossible to carry the same team into the next season. The Brewers may not be making many changes to their championship team, but some are coming. item.title: No. 2-seed Maryland field hockey dominates No. 6-seed Iowa, 4-1, in Big Ten Tournament semifinals
item.description: No. 2-seed Maryland field hockey has a knack for fast starts. Entering Friday’s Big Ten tournament semifinal against No. 6-seed Iowa, the Terps had outscored opponents by 11 in the first quarter. By the time the first 15 minutes had elapsed on Friday in Columbus, Ohio, the Terps added two more goals to the aforementioned total. Maryland’s fast start set the tone for what turned out to be a 4-1 demolition of Iowa. Like the teams’ regular-season matchup a week ago, Maryland jumped on Iowa for a quick score. Despite failures on its first two penalty corners, Maryland maintained pressure and eventually broke Iowa’s tight defense. Jordyn Hollamon used a brilliant backhanded shot from the left wing to the top right corner of the cage to get the offense started five minutes into the match. 10 minutes later, the Terps made it two in the first frame. On an unconventional penalty corner routine, Babs van Hest received the insertion, rotated to her right and attempted a shot towards the near post. The ball immediately clanked off an Iowa defender and was redirected over the head of Iowa goalkeeper Julia Claessens to make it 2-0. The early explosion was eerily similar to last Friday’s matchup. In the first meeting, Maryland scored three times in the opening quarter and forced Iowa to switch goalies. While Maryland only scored twice this time around, the Terps still forced Iowa’s hand. When the second quarter began, Abby Johnson was in net for the Hawkeyes. “I think it was the way we got the penalty corners. We used some nice deflections in the shell area that got into people’s feet,” said head coach Missy Meharg. “I think we were super creative, and [the players] believed that they could pick up each other’s balls that they just tipped in [the net].” Iowa settled down in the second quarter, holding Maryland’s offense to two shots and one corner while generating transition offense. As the quarter wound down, Iowa’s attack was at its best with relentless pressure in the shooting circle. However, the Hawkeyes couldn’t find the net, as goalkeeper Alyssa Klebasko and defender Josie Hollamon teamed up to make a trio of big-time denials and keep the Hawkeyes scoreless heading into the break. Hollamon especially was on her game. On a pair of occasions in that sequence, Klebasko was slightly out of position, but Hollamon was there to stop the ball’s advancements and distribute it to her teammates, who cleared the ball away from danger. Maryland came out the aggressor in the second half, creating four set pieces off the bat. It took all four of those corners, but the Terps eventually found their third goal of the affair. item.description: (Photo by Mitchell Leff/Getty Images) | Getty Images Las Vegas Raiders head coach Klint Kubiak made headlines during last week’s game against the New York Jets. Not for himself, but a decision he made with Las Vegas’ backfield. Kubiak didn’t just switch the Raiders’ lead running back between rookie Mike Washington Jr. and second-year pro Ashton Jeanty; he turned Washington into the feature back with 25 carries and made Jeanty the third-down option with just two carries and three catches. Now, heading into the Week 9 matchup against the San Francisco 49ers, the question arises of whether the workload split between Washington and Jeanty will continue . Some have speculated that Kubiak’s decision was punitive-based. Ahead of last week’s game, Jeanty gave the Jets ‘bulletin board material’ by saying that a few players on New York’s defense “don’t really want to tackle”. While the first-time head coach is still establishing his identity, he’s made it clear that he takes a ‘no-nonsense’ type of approach and doesn’t divulge much to the media to avoid situations like this. So, there’s reason to believe that the running back’s comments irked Kubiak and played a role in the former’s workload last Sunday. However, this Sunday will give us a better answer to see if the 25-to-2 (or 12.5-to-1) ratio of carries, or a similar type of split, continues. On Monday, the head coach indicated that the workload between the two backs could vary game to game. “I think it’s always a moving target,” he replied when asked if the Raiders will have a shared backfield moving forward. “See where your team’s at, and who’s playing the best ball at the time. And it’s a 17-game regular season where things change every week. And they’ve been changing at guard…That’s the NFL. “We have a young roster, and we’re going to give guys opportunities and see what fits us best. But your 11, whether you’re playing really well or not playing well at all, it’s always going to change a little bit.” Despite those comments, it’s hard to deny that the Raiders’ rushing attack did a better job of staying on schedule last week. Washington had 83 yards on his 25 carries, which comes out to 3.3 ypc. That’s pretty comparable to Jeanty’s 3.1 ypc for the season. But the rookie’s average was brought down by a handful of stuffed runs near the goal line. Also, Vegas’ EPA per rush was 0.11 points better last week than the team’s season average, and its success rate on the ground was 7.2% higher, per Sumer Sports . That being said, Washington’s lack of success in the red zone can’t be ignored. item.description: Nick Saban was asked about the College Football Playoff’s planned move to 24 teams on this week’s episode of New Heights, the podcast hosted by brothers Jason and Travis Kelce. The seven-time national champion coach, now an analyst on ESPN’s College GameDay, did not need long to answer. “Too many. There’s not 24 teams in the country that can win the national championship. So, what is the reason to actually do it? He’s got it. Yeah, but what you’re giving up, which is what I hate to see, is, you know, the SEC Championship Game playing the SEC Championship Game was a big thing to our players. It was a big thing to our fans. It was a tradition, and it was a great venue. I mean, there is only two teams that can play in a national championship, but more teams can play in those kinds of championship games, and there’s a lot of pride in winning the conference championship. And we’re going to give that up to have an extra game where the 24th team is going to play the ninth-best team. I’m not a big proponent of it. I think it minimizes the importance of the season,” Saban said. Ex Alabama head coach Nick Saban. (Credits – IMAGN) Yahoo Sports’ Ross Dellenger first reported in October that the CFP had reached a deal with ESPN to double the field starting with the 2027 season, and ESPN reported days later that the sides had a handshake agreement, though the contract has not been formally signed. Under the format Dellenger laid out , conference championship games go away, the top eight seeds get byes, and seeds 9 through 24 open with on-campus games in the second week of December. Only one spot is reserved, for the highest-ranked Group of Six champion, with the other 23 coming from the committee’s rankings. ESPN is expected to pay about $350 million more for the expanded postseason, according to Dellenger’s reporting, and after the roughly $200 million in lost conference title game revenue comes off the top, about $150 million is left for the conferences to split. item.description: Signage for the National Hockey League’s 2027 Winter Classic is displayed before a press conference held by the Utah Mammoth and NHL at Rice-Eccles Stadium in Salt Lake City on Wednesday, Jan. 7, 2026. | Isaac Hale, Deseret News Outdoor NHL games count the same as every other contest — two points in the standings. But that’s the last thing people remember about events like the Winter Classic. NHL president of content and events Steve Mayer and his team have spent the last year devising the best possible game-day experience for fans at the New Year’s Eve game between the Utah Mammoth and the Colorado Avalanche at Rice-Eccles Stadium. In an exclusive interview with the Deseret News, he laid out his plan. “What we’re building out is a bit of a winter wonderland,” Mayer said. “And there’s probably no better place to build that out than in Utah, given the proximity to the ski resorts. “We’re building out a ski resort on the field and in that stadium, and that’s sort of the overall look and feel for our game.” What does he mean when he says they’re building out a ski resort? He means they’re literally building an area to ski. There’s a large amount of open space between the rink and the stands, given the size disparity between a hockey rink and the football field that the stadium was built to house. The NHL is putting an actual, functioning cross-country skiing track in that space. The musician headlining the intermission show has yet to be announced, but the plan is for the artist to utilize the ski track while performing. Mayer’s team is also exploring the possibility of building either a ski lift or a mountain in the corner of the stadium, which he says is made possible because of the height of Rice-Eccles Stadium. item.description: Jay Stansfield's goal on Tuesday, Blues' third in their 3-0 home win against Millwall, was only his second of the season [Shutterstock] Birmingham City record signing Jay Stansfield may have only scored two goals so far this season - but the way Blues are playing, coupled with his own form, has him hoping that there are still plenty more to come. After his 12 Championship goals failed to prevent Blues being relegated in 2023-24, Stansfield then increased that number to 19 in League One to help win promotion when his loan signing from Fulham had been turned into a £15m move . He added 10 more in the Championship last season to help Blues finish 10th - and is now within one goal of becoming only the third Birmingham City player to reach 50 goals for the club in the past 40 seasons - to follow Paul Furlong (56) and Stansfield's former team-mate Lukas Jutkiewicz (69) in that respect. But he is now doing it in a very different role to when he first arrived at the club - and is very much enjoying playing as a foil to targetman August Priske, especially when, even without January signing Priske on the park, Max Bird set him up to score Blues' third goal in their early match-winning blitz at home to Millwall on Tuesday. That was Birmingham's fifth win in six games since the three-week international break - and they now head into Saturday's home test against Swansea City having overtaken the early Championship leaders as third plays fifth, with both teams on the same points. "We used the break to come together and work on a lot of things," Stansfield told BBC Radio WM. "And you can see the improvement of the whole team in general. The starters and the bench players." Triple injury boost for Swansea before Blues test Stewart hoping unlikely path leads back to top "The best teams are full of hungry players, raring to go," he added. "And everyone is in a good place. "It's important that other players are chipping in with the goals. All the players we've brought on have done well. And it's so good to have direct wingers like Liam Millar and Demarai Gray who look to score goals." Full-back Alex Cochrane got his second goal in successive games in the win over Millwall, before August signing Bird claimed his first. "Different people have been scoring, which helps us as forwards knowing someone else can step up and score," said Stansfield. "The last few games I've really enjoyed and I'm developing more and more. "Last season we were playing out from the back a lot, but now we're playing into a big striker in August. Our connection and understanding can only get better too. "I used to love in my academy days getting on the ball and making things happen. I like to peel off the shoulder and get balls played in behind, and last season I wasn't doing much of that. "Being the second striker and feeding off August, I've had some really good chances. As long as I'm getting chances, that's key. Now I've got one I can kick on."

item.description: Referees, ranked contenders, a leaderboard, and even a commissioner are overseeing the entire operation. Welcome to the Los Angeles Rams shadow boxing league, where the competition is fierce, the trash talk is plentiful and the bragging rights might be worth more than the championship itself. Oh, and at the center of it all is the reigning NFL Defensive Player of the Year, who also happens to be the undisputed champion of the league. Instead of retreating into their phones between meetings, players are challenging teammates, laughing, talking trash and building relationships that extend beyond their position groups. Getty Images What initially started as a harmless way to kill some time between meetings has blossomed into a full-fledged locker room phenomenon, bringing players together during a season filled with injuries, adversity and enormous expectations. Rams linebacker Grant Stuard is the self-appointed commissioner, who has turned a childhood-style game into something resembling the UFC. “We thought it’d be cool to get some organization going and get a league started,” Stuard told the California Post in an exclusive interview Thursday. Stuard and teammate Matthew Caldwell helped establish a running leaderboard that now features a top 10, position-group rankings and honorable mentions. Even injured players have found their way onto the board. But at this point you’re probably asking yourself the same question we did: What exactly is shadow boxing? Despite its name, nobody is throwing any actual punches. Two players stand face-to-face. One points up, down, left or right while the other simultaneously moves his head in a direction, hoping to avoid looking where his opponent points. If the movements match, the attacker scores. Players alternate turns, attempting to anticipate each other’s reactions and string together successful moves. It’s part reflexes, part mind games and entirely addictive. Throughout the season, easily over half the Rams locker room has participated. And because NFL players apparently can’t compete at anything without turning it into its own organized sport, Stuard has established official rules. Ranked matches are best-of-three and require a witness or referee. Matchups involving the top three competitors require two officials. “If it’s a top-three ranked match, you need two refs,” Stuard explained. “You have to have some standards of what’s acceptable play.” The rankings operate similar to the UFC’s weight class rankings. An unranked player can challenge a ranked contender, and if the higher-ranked player accepts and loses, the leaderboard gets reshuffled. Kansas City Chiefs Hall of Fame Center Tim Grunhard Calls Out Creed Humphrey for Errant Snaps @grunny61 talked about Kahlil Benson being the right tackle of the future & Creed Humphrey's snap issues with us on @ArrowheadAllies. pic.twitter.com/g1n2efxHuO — Starcade Media (@StarcadeMediaKC) November 5, 2026 Humphrey is a three-time All-Pro, making his issues with snapping the ball puzzling. Former Chiefs center Tim Grunhard, who was inducted into the team’s Hall of Fame in 2021, sounded off over Humphrey’s errant snaps while joining the folks at Starcade Media. “Communication is important, blocking the guy in front of you is important, finishing plays is important, but the most important thing is to get the ball to the damn quarterback,” Grunhard said. “That’s your job, it’s as simple as that. When you’re not doing it correctly, it’s like giving up a sack. It’s like having a missed assignment. It screws the play up. I’ve talked to him over the years. I’m sure he knows I’ve said it before. The reality is, your number one responsibility is to get the ball to the quarterback in a timely fashion.” Grunhard Praises Kahlil Benson Although Benson has had some struggles, he is doing better than most expected . Benson is an undrafted free agent, and did not play left tackle at all during his collegiate days. As good as you can ask from him. He’s a right tackle. He’s more of a mauler, he’s a physical football player. I do think he struggles against some speed rushes, but he’s done a good job. item.title: LaVell’s trust, confidence fueled Brandon Doman’s belief that he could win
item.description: BYU’s Brandon Doman goes head-to-head with Utah’s Arnold Parker during the Utah v. BYU game at Rice Eccles Stadium at the University of Utah on Friday, November 24, 2000. | JOHANNA WORKMAN Editor’s note: Eighth in an occasional series exploring LaVell Edwards’ legacy of leadership. No player who suited up for LaVell Edwards faced more immediate pressure to succeed than Brandon Doman. Injuries to the other quarterbacks opened the door for Doman to make his first start at BYU in the last home game for his legendary coach. Doman had dreamed of this opportunity ever since he was old enough to hold a football. He waited patiently for his moment — and it was finally here. “I had seen him put all of his effort and energy behind a quarterback before, and in that moment, I knew I had Lavell Edwards in my corner, and when he said, ‘You’re my guy,’ he was going to give me every shot,” Doman said. “So, I walked out of his office with the utmost confidence that he believed in me, and that I could go lead the football team. I don’t know that there’s any quarterback that played at BYU that’s walked out of his office, having been told, ‘You’re my guy,’ who didn’t feel that way.” Adding to the pressure of the moment, which included a pesky New Mexico team, was the fact that at 4-6, BYU was on the cusp of sending Edwards into retirement with his first losing season since 1972 — four years before his new quarterback was born. Doman needed to go 2-0 to keep that from happening. In addition, Gordon B. Hinckley, President of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, stopped by the locker room to give the team a pregame pep talk that included his famous line: “Don’t muff it!” “I think when that moment occurred, the prophet was there, who I loved, President Hinckley, and Lavell Edwards. I mean, I can’t think of two more iconic people in the year 2000 for a member of the church than those two, and there we were, standing and surrounding them, shoulder to shoulder, and in kind of a sacred moment with the prophet, and also this, you know, war cry to go out and play the greatest game of all time. “I felt both the spirit and the power of calmness that it brought.
